target_customer: Consumers wanting to buy, sell and hold bitcoin, and merchants wanting to accept it; later institutions
problem: In 2012 buying bitcoin meant wiring money to offshore exchanges such as Mt. Gox, and storing it safely was hard. Coinbase offered a US bank-linked buy and sell flow plus a simple wallet and merchant tools.
business_model: Transaction fee on buys and sells, merchant processing, later custody, staking and institutional services

founders.name: Brian Armstrong
founders.background_notes: Former Airbnb engineer per a Wikipedia mirror; the YC page lists only him as founder.

founders.name: Fred Ehrsam
founders.background_notes: Former Goldman Sachs trader; named as co-founder in the 2013 funding coverage.

technical_complexity.rationale: Handling custody and bank linking for a volatile new asset meant security and fraud engineering, but no research breakthroughs were needed.

defensibility.rationale: Early US bank rails and money transmitter licensing gave a lead, though the product idea was copyable; trust became the main asset.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No large incumbent cared in 2012. Mt. Gox failed in 2014 and Coinbase grew into the largest US exchange.

market_need_then: Bitcoin was tiny in 2012 but exchanges were hard for ordinary US users. By December 2013 Coinbase reported about 600,000 wallets and over 16,000 merchants, showing demand.

branding.domain_note: Operates on coinbase.com; the separate exchange site was later merged into it (Bitcoin Wiki).

identity.logo: Blue wordmark; early versions carried a beta tag and a coin inspired symbol per logo history sites
identity.visual_style: Clean blue and white fintech look
identity.voice_and_tone: Plain and trust focused; the company states it wants to be the most trusted in its domain

branding.brand_signature: Blue wordmark tied to trusted entry point into crypto

rebrands.why: Exchange product renamed; one low authority source, later folded back into coinbase.com

brand_strength.rationale: Became a household name for buying crypto and the first crypto firm to list directly in April 2021; evidence is from press coverage of the listing, not brand research.

outcome_analysis: Coinbase rode the growth of bitcoin and later crypto, built a regulated and trusted US on ramp while offshore exchanges failed, raised a $25M Series B led by Andreessen Horowitz in December 2013 and listed directly on Nasdaq in April 2021. It now faces regulatory and shareholder litigation, and its fortunes track crypto cycles.
